prompt: Why are stop criteria written before the release starts?

choices.text: Because the pipeline cannot read files during a release
choices.why: It reads them whenever it runs.

choices.text: So the decision is made calmly, once
choices.why: Right. Nobody argues with the numbers mid-incident.

choices.text: So the release goes faster
choices.why: Speed is not what they buy.

choices.text: Because a canary cannot be stopped once started
choices.why: The script stops it at any step.

prompt: Match each constant in canary.py to the question it answers.

pairs.right: How much worse is too much?

prompt: How many requests does canary.py send at each step?
The criteria live in a file in the repository. What does that make visible?

choices.text: Which customers met the canary
choices.why: The file holds rules, not traffic.

choices.text: How long each release took
choices.why: That lives in the pipeline's history.

choices.text: Loosening them to get one release out
choices.why: Right. It goes through a pull request like any change.

choices.text: The error rate of the last canary
choices.why: The script prints that; the file does not keep it.

prompt: At 5%, green answered 21 requests. What did canary.py do?

choices.text: Aborted, because the sample was too small to be safe
choices.why: A small sample is a reason to wait, not to stop.

choices.text: Said it was too few to judge, and went on
choices.why: Right. 21 is under MIN_REQUESTS.

choices.text: Promoted green, since it had no errors
choices.why: Promotion comes only after the last step.

choices.text: Sent another 400 requests at 5%
choices.why: It moves to the next step.

prompt: At which share, in percent, did canary.py abort 1.6.0?
What does canary.py's exit code 1 do in a pipeline?

choices.text: It restarts the canary from 5%
choices.why: Nothing reruns it.

choices.text: It rolls blue back to the previous release
choices.why: Blue was never changed.

choices.text: It deletes green's release directory
choices.why: Green stays, to be examined.

choices.text: It fails the job; nothing after it runs
choices.why: Right. The pipeline reads the code and stops.

prompt: With MAX_GAP at 1.0, what does the rule really do between 50 and 99 answers?
hint: Work out the rate of one error in 98 answers.

choices.text: It stops on the first error
choices.why: Right. One in 98 is 1.02%, over the gap.

choices.text: It ignores errors until 100 answers
choices.why: It judges from 50.

choices.text: It needs at least two errors to stop
choices.why: One is enough below 100 answers.

choices.text: It compares latency instead of errors
choices.why: It only counts errors.

prompt: Which are honest fixes for that flaw, by the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Raise MIN_REQUESTS until one error cannot cross the gap
choices.why: Right. Bugs are then caught later.

choices.text: Use a statistical test instead of a fixed gap
choices.why: Right. It asks whether the difference beats chance.

choices.text: Rerun an aborted canary until it passes
choices.why: A rule overridden whenever it fires is not a rule.

choices.text: Remove MIN_REQUESTS
choices.why: Then a single request could decide.

prompt: Across its four steps, how many requests did green answer when 1.6.1 was promoted?
hint: Add green's count at each step.

prompt: What does a clean canary show about the new release?

choices.text: That it is correct
choices.why: It measured errors, not correctness.

choices.text: That it is not worse, at what was measured
choices.why: Right. What was not measured was not checked.

choices.text: That its prices match the carrier's
choices.why: Nothing compared prices.

choices.text: That blue can be deleted
choices.why: Blue stays until slow problems have had time to show.

prompt: 1.6.1's canary counted only errors. Which bug would it have promoted?

choices.text: A KeyError on one CEP prefix
choices.why: That is a 500, and it was counted.

choices.text: A process that crashes at start
choices.why: The smoke test catches that first.

choices.text: Every quote a 200 with a wrong price
choices.why: Right. Only a business metric would notice.

choices.text: A port number typed wrong in config.env
choices.why: The deploy's smoke test fails on it.

prompt: What does ops/rollback.sh change on disk?

choices.text: It swaps two links
choices.why: Right. current and previous trade places, then it restarts and smokes.

choices.text: It unpacks the previous artifact again
choices.why: It is still unpacked in releases/.

choices.text: It reverts the last commit
choices.why: It never touches git.

choices.text: It rewrites config.env
choices.why: Configuration belongs to the environment and stays.

prompt: How many seconds did the rollback take, to the nearest tenth?
What made the rollback fast? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The old release was still on disk
choices.why: Right. Nothing had to be fetched.

choices.text: Nothing was built
choices.why: Right. The same artifact that ran before ran again.

choices.text: The configuration stayed where it was
choices.why: Right. Only the code moved.

choices.text: The restart skipped the smoke test
choices.why: It ran the smoke test.

prompt: Why is rebuilding 1.5.0 from its tag not the same as rolling back to it?

choices.text: Git tags cannot be checked out
choices.why: They can.

choices.text: The rebuild is a new artifact that never ran
choices.why: Right. Lesson 7: build once, deploy those bytes.

choices.text: The tag points at 1.6.0 after the release
choices.why: A tag does not move.

choices.text: 1.5.0 cannot read 1.6.0's configuration
choices.why: The configuration did not change.

prompt: Production runs 1.5.0 after one rollback. Somebody runs rollback.sh again. What runs now?

choices.text: 1.5.0 still; the script refuses to roll back twice
choices.why: It swaps the links every time.

choices.text: The release before 1.5.0
choices.why: It remembers one step only.

choices.text: 1.6.0, the release with the bug
choices.why: Right. A second rollback undoes the first.

choices.text: Nothing; the process is stopped
choices.why: It restarts and passes the smoke test.

prompt: After its first deploy, rollback.sh says the environment has no ___ release.
What do teams that trust their rollback do? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Run it in staging regularly
choices.why: Right. A rollback that ran last week works.

choices.text: Check what it will go back to first
choices.why: Right. readlink answers it in the lab.

choices.text: Name one person to call it
choices.why: Right. Two people at once is the double rollback.

choices.text: Keep it secret, so nobody runs it by mistake
choices.why: A path nobody knows is a path nobody can use.

prompt: Was 1.6.1 a rollback or a roll forward from 1.6.0?

choices.text: A rollback, because it removed code
choices.why: It added a test and a flag.

choices.text: A roll forward: a fix in a new release
choices.why: Right. One character, released as 1.6.1.

choices.text: Neither, it was a hotfix
choices.why: A hotfix shipped as a release is a roll forward.

choices.text: A rollback, because its number is close to 1.6.0
choices.why: Numbers say nothing about direction.

prompt: When is rolling forward the better choice, by the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The release before is broken too
choices.why: Right. Going back one step fixes nothing.

choices.text: Going back would undo a migration the old release cannot read
choices.why: Right. The next section covers those.

choices.text: The fix is small and the pipeline is as fast as a rollback
choices.why: Right. Then both reach production as quickly.

choices.text: The author of the change prefers it
choices.why: That is the argument a default removes.

prompt: Why is "roll back first" a good default during an incident?

choices.text: Rollbacks never fail
choices.why: Section 06 showed two ways they surprise.

choices.text: It stops the damage before the cause is known
choices.why: Right. The fix can then be written the usual way.

choices.text: It avoids writing a postmortem
choices.why: The postmortem is written either way.

choices.text: Customers prefer older versions
choices.why: Customers did not ask.

prompt: Which of these does a rollback leave behind? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A migration that changed the schema
choices.why: Right. The old code meets the new schema.

choices.text: E-mails already sent
choices.why: Right. Rolling back stops only the next ones.

choices.text: Messages in a shared queue
choices.why: Right. The old consumers meet them.

choices.text: The new release's code
choices.why: That is the one thing it does undo.

prompt: Order the releases of an expand-and-contract column change.
items: Stop writing the old column and drop it
trap: Dropping the old column is last: until then a rollback still needs it.

prompt: Which question does the lesson ask at review time for a release that touches state?

choices.text: How many tests cover the migration?
choices.why: Coverage says nothing about what stays behind.

choices.text: If rolled back an hour later, what is left behind?
choices.why: Right. Anything left needs a plan or a flag.

choices.text: Can it be deployed at night?
choices.why: The hour changes nothing about state.

choices.text: Who wrote the migration?
choices.why: The author changes nothing about state.

prompt: Run against 1.6.0's quote.py, the regression test failed with: assert [ ___ ] == [].
Why was the test run on the code with the bug as well as on the fix?

choices.text: To measure how long the suite takes
choices.why: Timing was not the point.

choices.text: A test never seen failing proves nothing yet
choices.why: Right. Red on the bug, green on the fix.

choices.text: Because pytest needs two runs to cache results
choices.why: It does not.

choices.text: To prove the old tests were wrong
choices.why: They were right, and incomplete.

prompt: The four-example test passed on 1.6.0. What does the regression test check instead?

choices.text: A fifth example, in Alagoas
choices.why: That catches 57 and nothing else.

choices.text: The response time of a quote to the Northeast
choices.why: It does not time anything.

choices.text: A property: every prefix has an estimate
choices.why: Right. It catches any gap a future edit leaves.

choices.text: That the app answers 500 for Alagoas
choices.why: That would test the bug, not the fix.

prompt: What does a blameless postmortem name?

choices.text: The person who wrote the line with the bug
choices.why: That is a cause nobody can act on.

choices.text: What happened, and what changes
choices.why: Right. A test, a flag and a rule.

choices.text: The reviewer who missed it
choices.why: Same: not a change anybody can make.

choices.text: The customers it affected
choices.why: They are counted, not named.

prompt: Which of these are changes, in the postmortem's sense? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A regression test for every prefix
choices.why: Right. Done in 1.6.1.

choices.text: The estimate behind a flag
choices.why: Right. It can be turned off without a deploy.

choices.text: Releases go out as canaries
choices.why: Right. With this lesson's criteria.

choices.text: Ana promises to be more careful
choices.why: "Be more careful" is not a change.

prompt: At 99.9% over 30 days, how many minutes of downtime does the budget allow?
The error budget for the month is spent. What does the rule say?

choices.text: Pause features; fix reliability
choices.why: Right. They resume when the budget recovers.

choices.text: Lower the objective to 99%
choices.why: Moving the target to fit is the opposite of the rule.

choices.text: Release faster to fix things sooner
choices.why: Releases are what spends the budget.

choices.text: Nothing, the budget is only a report
choices.why: It is a rule about releasing.

prompt: A team has not spent any of its error budget in a year. What does the lesson read into that?

choices.text: The objective should be raised to 100%
choices.why: No service reaches 100%, and trying costs without end.

choices.text: It releases too slowly, or aims too high
choices.why: Right. The budget is there to be spent.

choices.text: The canary criteria are too loose
choices.why: Loose criteria would spend the budget, not save it.

choices.text: Its tests can be removed
choices.why: The tests are part of why it is unspent.

prompt: Order what a team does when a release misbehaves, as this lesson teaches.
items: Stop it: abort the canary or roll back
Find the cause in the logs
Write a test that fails on the bug
Ship the fix as a new release
trap: Stopping comes before diagnosing: the damage grows while the cause is studied.

prompt: Match each tool of the lesson to what it decides.
Which part of the incident would a rollback alone not have fixed?

choices.text: The failing quotes to Alagoas
choices.why: Rolling back to 1.5.0 stopped them.

choices.text: The 500s in green's log
choices.why: Green out of traffic logs no more.

choices.text: The gap in the tests
choices.why: Right. The gap that let it through; only the regression test closes it.

choices.text: The time customers waited for a quote
choices.why: Blue answered at its usual speed.
